ours.name: East Face
ours.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (~3,400 ft, reached via ~8.7 mi of Icicle Creek Road southwest of Leavenworth), follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left (south) at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (this junction is also where the Lake Stuart fork continues straight); the trail crosses Mountaineer Creek on a log/boulder crossing that can be a wet, awkward ford in early season high water. Continue climbing through forest and over a boulder field to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3 miles from the trailhead — this is the last reliable, easily accessed water source and most parties treat water here before pushing on. It is the only known way to climb 9 peaks of the Washington Bulgers 100 tallest list in a single day. Previously, such peakbagging endeavors were multi-day expeditions into the heart of the Enchantments, requiring a hard to acquire overnight permit. Note: As fastestknowntime.com seeks to support local permit systems, abiding the rules means in attempting this FKT you will not sleep inside of the permit zone at any point during your FKT attempt, regardless of your success or failure, without acquiring the permit through the lottery system . This link-up is the foremost exquisite display of some of the best climbing, terrain, ridge traversing, and views the Enchantments have to offer. Consider it fair warning that Tyler researched and rehearsed every element of this peak link-up before managing to put it all together in under 24 hours, car-to-car. ours.name: East Ridge (Inspiration Glacier)
ours.approach: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. fktText: Description https://www.summitpost.org/eldorado-peak/150316 Eldorado Peak (8876') is Located in the North Cascades National Park and is on the Washington Top 100 list. Fred Beckey calls this peak "Queen of the Cascade River" considering that it is in the middle of a collection of beautiful peaks. Massively aloof, perched at the edge of the largest contiguous ice-sheet in the lower 48 states not connected to a volcano, the summit has a Himalayan like splendor owing to its remoteness, position, and knife-edge summit ridge. The total climb encompasses a 6,800 feet of vertical feet (not including ups and downs) and can be made through one of two interesting approaches. The climb is not technically difficult, and a number of people climb up each year to experience the thrill of stamping out a "just-wide-enough" path on the summit ridge and looking into the heart of the Klawatti-Inspiration-McAlister icecap. Views into Marble Creek, Dorado Needle, Forbidden Peak, Mount Buckner, Logan, Johannesburg and the other peaks of the Ptarmigan Traverse. It is an exhilarating summit experience, the ridge gives one a feeling of being out in the true alpine environment. This is a mountain that any mountaineer visiting the Pacific Northwest really should see and climb it! East Ridge : This is considered to be the Standard Route up Eldorado Peak because it has the lesser distance approach, the least amount of work, and is non technical. ours.name: Northwest Couloir / Eldorado Glacier
ours.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. ours.descent: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing

ours.name: North Ridge
ours.approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to high camp on the Inspiration Glacier, then cross the Inspiration Glacier around the east end of the East Ridge and traverse the glacier on the mountain's north side at about 8,100 ft to the NW Ice Couloir notch at the base of the North Ridge.
ours.descent: Return down the same ridge system to the notch and back to camp on the Inspiration Glacier; parties who finish via the East Ridge instead descend that ridge's knife-edge back to camp.

ours.name: Northeast Face
ours.approach: Same as the East Ridge: Eldorado Creek trailhead (2,100 ft) via Cascade River Road, boulder field, Eldorado Creek basin, and the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier to around 7,500-8,200 ft, where the Northeast Face angles off climbers' right of the standard glacier track.
ours.descent: Descend the standard East Ridge rather than the face. ours.name: West Arete
ours.approach: Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, camp near the base of the East Ridge (about 7,500 ft), then cross the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers to Dorado Needle Col and make a loose fourth-class downclimb into the Marble Creek cirque, traversing to the toe of the arete near 6,000 ft. Typically a 3-day trip (approach day, climb day, exit day); the first roughly 800 ft of climbing is Class 4 before harder 5th-class sections.
ours.descent: From the summit, descend the East Ridge — most parties find this significantly easier and more straightforward than downclimbing the loose West Arete — then return to camp via the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier.

ours.name: Enchantment Enchainment
ours.approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake trail up Mountaineer Creek through old burn toward Stuart Lake. Beyond the lake leave the trail and climb the slopes, then steep snow, to the notch on Stuart's northwest face that gives the shortcut onto the upper West Ridge. The West Ridge is normally approached from the south, so this north-side access sees little traffic; expect snow in the notch and gully well into summer.
ours.descent: Two ways out from Cannon. The direct line drops north off Cannon straight toward the Stuart Lake trail and the trailhead: roughly 5,000 vertical ft of loose dirt, talus and cliff bands in the upper half, then steep brush and unmapped cliff bands in the lower 2,000 ft, which is slow and miserable, especially in the dark. The longer but known alternative is to return across the Core to Aasgard Pass

ours.name: Disappointment Peak Cleaver (Gerdine Ridge / Cool Glacier)
ours.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,050 ft, off FR 49/Sloan Creek Road), hike ~9 mi to White Pass on the PCT. Continue east on the Foam Creek Trail ~2 mi, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, then traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending NE to Glacier Gap (~7,300 ft), the standard high camp where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet. Summit day is roughly 7 mi round trip with about 3,450 ft of gain, some of it height lost and regained along the way: climb gentle snow above camp, follow a climber's track on volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers, end-run a crevasse or two, then rejoin the climber's trail for the final steep pitch to the summit.
ours.descent: No rappelling; reverse the ascent line on foot. From the summit, descend the ridge to the 9,600 ft col, then down the Cool Glacier to the 9,100 ft col. On the traverse back beneath Disappointment Peak, keep lower and farther from the face than on the way in to cut the time spent under its rockfall. fktText: Description summitpost.org : Glacier Peak (10,541') is one of the five volcanoes of the state of Washington, and is the highest mountain in Snohomish county. It has 7498 feet of prominence and ranks 5th highest on the Bulgar List (Washington Top 100) . It is located in the North Central part of the Cascades which it has a wilderness named after this mountain which is called the Glacier Peak Wilderness . The Native Americans once called this peak Takobia which would translate to "The Great Parent". This peak is classified as a stratovolcanoe (Composite) which there has not been any major activity in 300 years. This peak goes unnoticed by much of the people of the Northwest due to it being so far in the crest of the Cascades, its distance from the nearest town, and the fact that its access roads have been washed out making all the approaches to its base a long hike in. Glacier Peak can be seen from many locations along the Mountain Loop Highway , North Cascades , Highway 2 area, and many other high points through out the state. But this peak is often hidden from view from many low land areas which is another big reason it goes unnoticed by many. The summit offers amazing views of many of the great peaks of Washington, as well as a view of seeing far across the state. ours.name: Frostbite Ridge
ours.approach: Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via the White Chuck River, no longer usable since a 2003 flood destroyed the trail and road: the old line followed the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing (water) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT on Glacier Ridge about 0.7 miles beyond the creek, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. ours.name: Kennedy Glacier
ours.approach: Standard historical approach: from the White Chuck River Trailhead (FS-23, closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 after flood damage; check status), follow trail #643 about 4 miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the PCT; turn left (north) and follow the PCT about 2 miles to the Glacier Creek crossing and campsites (pack-in time 4-5 hours). An alternate approach via the North Fork Sauk Trail and PCT over Red Pass to Glacier Creek is also used and is the open option while FS-23 stays closed.
ours.descent: Besides reversing the ascent line, the standard alternate descent goes via Frostbite Ridge: traverse past the distinctive 'Rabbit Ears' rock formation, then descend the (separate) Vista Glacier back down to the lower Kennedy Glacier and Kennedy Ridge camp, watching for opened crevasses and softening snow bridges throughout.
